html:
The Barkindji, or Paakantyi, are an Aboriginal Australian people who live along the Darling River in far west New South Wales. They call the river the Baaka, and their name means people of the river. The map shows them from 1600 to 1800.

The Darling winds for hundreds of kilometres through dry plains, and the river, its lakes and its floodplains gave fish, waterbirds, mussels and seed foods. Around the Menindee Lakes there are old campsites, shell middens and burials.

The explorer Charles Sturt reached the Darling in 1829, and steamers and wool stations followed later in the century. The Burke and Wills expedition set up its depot at Menindee in 1860. In 2015 a court recognised Barkindji native title over a large part of far west New South Wales. Neighbours on the map include the Barindji, the Danggali and the Wilyakali. See Aboriginal Australian societies.
